questions.title: Section A — Question 1 (Case study: hominid evolution, Little Foot and Sterkfontein)

subQuestions.questionText:
The source describes hominid fossils from Sterkfontein (Little Foot / Australopithecus prometheus), 'Lucy' (Australopithecus afarensis), the work of Raymond Dart and Philip Tobias, and cladograms of hominid relationships. Describe the meaning of the following terms:
1.1.1 Hominid
1.1.2 Evolution
subQuestions.memoText:
1.1.1 (2 marks): a (bipedal) primate / fossil showing a mixture of ape-like and human-like characteristics — humans and their close extinct relatives.
1.1.2 (2 marks): the cumulative genetic changes in a population over time / the process by which different kinds of living organisms developed from earlier forms during the history of the Earth, brought about by natural selection, genetic drift and environmental change.

subQuestions.questionText:
'Lucy' is a famous example of an extinct hominid species.
1.2.1 What is the scientific name of the fossil known as 'Lucy'?
1.2.2 Use the information in the text on page v (the relevant dates given are 3 670 000 years and 500 000 years) to calculate how long ago Lucy had been alive. Show all working.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.2.1 Australopithecus afarensis (1).
1.2.2 3 670 000 − 500 000 = 3 170 000 years ago (2 marks; mark given for identifying the correct values even if the method is wrong).

subQuestions.questionText:
There were two hypotheses to explain how Little Foot ended up in the cave, but only one has scientific support.
1.3.1 What is a hypothesis?
1.3.2 (a) Which one of the two hypotheses has the most support?
(b) Use information in the text to justify your choice.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.3.1 (2 marks): a testable statement / proposed explanation or predicted outcome regarding a scientific phenomenon or the relationship between variables.
1.3.2 (a) Hypothesis 1 — that Little Foot fell into the cave and died there (rather than being carried or washed in) (1).
(b) (2 marks): the bones were still articulated (connected together), which would not be the case if predators had pulled the body apart or if it had decomposed and been scattered; there are no predator tooth marks / damage on the bones; the skeleton is in one place, not spread out as it would be if washed in over time.

subQuestions.questionText:
For each name, decide which item relates to it. Write '1' if only the first item relates to the name, '2' if only the second, or 'none' if neither.
1.4.1 Raymond Dart. Item 1: Mrs Ples. Item 2: Taung Child.
1.4.2 Homo habilis. Item 1: 'Handy man'. Item 2: Quadrupedal.
1.4.3 Homo erectus. Item 1: Brain is bigger than Homo sapiens's. Item 2: Foramen magnum at the back of the skull.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.4.1 2 — Raymond Dart described the Taung Child (Mrs Ples was found by Robert Broom).
1.4.2 1 — Homo habilis means 'handy man'; it was bipedal, not quadrupedal.
1.4.3 none — Homo erectus had a smaller brain than Homo sapiens, and its foramen magnum was positioned centrally (under the skull), not at the back.
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Australopithecus prometheus appears to be a bipedal hominid but still shows many quadrupedal characteristics (Figure 1.6, the skeleton of Little Foot).
1.5.1 Discuss ONE environmental factor that would have made bipedalism an advantage for Australopithecus prometheus.
1.5.2 Suggest ONE feature that Prof. Clarke would have used to conclude that Australopithecus prometheus was most likely bipedal.
1.5.3 (a) Provide ONE quadrupedal feature present in Little Foot.
(b) Explain why the feature you mentioned in 1.5.3(a) indicates quadrupedal behaviour.
(Refer to Figure 1.6 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
1.5.1 (2 marks — one factor + its advantage): long grass / open grassland — standing upright lets the animal see over the grass to spot predators or prey; loss of forest / more open ground — bipedal walking is more energy-efficient over long distances; more sun exposure / less shade — an upright body exposes less skin surface to the sun.
1.5.2 (1): a bowl-shaped pelvis / long legs / the foramen magnum positioned vertically below the skull / evidence of an upright posture.
1.5.3 (a) (1): large shoulder blades (scapulae) / long arms / a divergent (opposable) big toe.
(b) (2): e.g. a divergent big toe is used to grip branches, showing tree-climbing (arboreal) behaviour; long arms and large scapulae give attachment for powerful arm muscles used in climbing or knuckle-walking rather than for walking on two legs.

subQuestions.questionText: Philip Tobias stated that 'it is a deeply important political fact that life began in Africa'. What did he mean by this statement?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): because humans originated in Africa, the rest of the world must recognise Africa as scientifically and historically important (rather than seeing it as contributing nothing); it directly contradicts apartheid, racist and colonialist ideas that Africans are 'behind' or 'less developed' than Europeans; it places Africa at the centre of the human story.

subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the cladogram in Figure 1.8 (hominid relationships), with unlabelled positions A, B and C.
1.7.1 Which hominid is still living?
1.7.2 How long ago did Homo erectus and Australopithecus africanus share a common ancestor?
1.7.3 At which position on the cladogram (point A, B or C) would Australopithecus prometheus most likely be placed?
(Refer to Figure 1.8 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
1.7.1 Homo sapiens (1).
1.7.2 About 3,3–3,4 million years ago (1).
1.7.3 B (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why scientists need to work carefully during the excavation of fossils from the Sterkfontein Caves.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): the bones are embedded in hard breccia and must be separated from the rock slowly so that rock and bone are not confused; the bones are very fragile and easily damaged; the fossils are scientifically very valuable and irreplaceable, so any damage is a serious loss; caves are dangerous (rockfalls), so care is needed for safety too.

questions.title: Section A — Question 2 (Case study: stick insect evolution and speciation)

subQuestions.questionText:
The source describes stick insects on Lord Howe Island and New Caledonia, hypotheses of convergent evolution, DNA and fossil evidence, cladograms, and speciation from a small founding population. Study Figure 2.4 (photographs of different species of stick insect, one with a scale line AB).
2.1.1 Describe what is meant by the caption 'different species of stick insect'.
2.1.2 Calculate the actual length of the New Caledonia stick insect by using the line AB next to the photo (line AB measures 31 mm and represents a scale factor of 0,3). Show all working and give your answer in mm.
(Refer to Figure 2.4 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
2.1.1 (2 marks): different groups of stick insects that cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring with one another.
2.1.2 (3 marks): 31 mm ÷ 0,3 = 103,3 mm (working + answer with unit).

subQuestions.questionText: One hypothesis for the evolution of the specific features of the Lord Howe stick insect was that it occurred by convergent evolution. What is meant by the term 'convergent evolution'?
subQuestions.memoText: 3 marks: when similar-looking (analogous) structures with the same function evolve in different organisms that do not share a recent common ancestor — the structures are not genetically the same and do not have a common evolutionary origin.

subQuestions.questionText: Describe the selection pressure that resulted in the convergent evolution in these stick insects.
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: the two locations had similar environments (e.g. similar forested habitat / climate) and therefore similar selection pressures, so natural selection favoured the same advantageous characteristics in both populations.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why DNA evidence is more accurate than fossil evidence for establishing relatedness amongst organisms.
subQuestions.memoText: At least one point for DNA reliability + one for fossil unreliability + one further point (3 marks): all organisms have DNA, and DNA is built from the same nucleotides in every species, so a similar DNA sequence between two organisms directly shows they are related; fossil evidence relies on structural similarity, which may be analogous rather than homologous (and fossils can be misidentified); not all organisms fossilise, and fossils are rare and hard to find and extract.

subQuestions.questionText:
Study the three cladograms (A, B and C) and the table of results on page x of the Source Material Booklet. Based on the results of the experiment, which cladogram, A, B or C, is the most accurate representation of the relationship amongst the four species?
(Refer to the cladograms and results table in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: B (2 marks) — it matches the pattern of DNA similarity shown in the results table.

subQuestions.questionText:
Study the sequence of fossils and the information about environmental changes in New Caledonia in Figure 2.5. Can the evolution of stick insects in New Caledonia be regarded as an example of punctuated equilibrium or as an example of gradualism? Justify your answer.
(Refer to Figure 2.5 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: 3 marks: punctuated equilibrium — the environment stayed the same for long periods with little change in the species' characteristics, and rapid change occurred only when the environment changed dramatically (rather than slow, continuous change, which would be gradualism).

subQuestions.questionText:
The Lord Howe stick insect evolved from a small population of stick insects that arrived on Lord Howe Island.
(a) Explain how the small size of the founding population contributed to the genetic differences seen in the Lord Howe population.
(b) From the points below, write the letters of the correct statements in the order in which evolution occurred:
A Acquired characteristics are passed on to the next generation.
B Over time characteristics diverged between the population on Lord Howe Island and the original population.
C Individuals acquired adaptations over their lifetime.
D Individuals with characteristics that were favourable on Lord Howe Island survived and reproduced.
E The original population mated with another species on the island.
F Individuals from the two new populations did not recognise one another as potential mates.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) (3 marks): the small founding population did not carry the same allele frequencies as the original population (it had less genetic variation); some alleles were absent, or more or less common than in the source population; so the new population's characteristics differed from the start — this is the founder effect.
(b) (3 marks): D → B → F.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why this type of speciation can be regarded as allopatric speciation and not sympatric speciation.
subQuestions.memoText: 3 marks: speciation occurred because the two populations were separated by a geographic barrier (they were on different islands), which prevented gene flow between them; sympatric speciation would occur in the same area with no geographic barrier to gene flow.

subQuestions.questionText: A plan has been put forward to remove the exotic species from Lord Howe Island. Suggest ONE reason why exotic species pose a threat to indigenous species.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one (1 mark): exotic species outcompete indigenous species for food, water or living space; they prey on and kill indigenous species; they use resources more effectively; and they often have no natural predators to keep their numbers in check.

subQuestions.questionText: Why is it important to establish World Heritage Sites such as the one on Lord Howe Island?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): it protects a unique natural environment and prevents development or building that would destroy the ecosystems; it raises the area's status and recognition as worth conserving (politically and internationally); it increases tourism; it gives inhabitants a sense of pride.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Sources A–H in the Source Material Booklet (the effects of climate change; the difficulty of saving every species; historical mass extinctions and recovery; evolved resistance in amphibians, killifish, corals and owls; keystone species; the London Underground mosquito and human-driven speciation; artificial selection of heat-tolerant corals; and rates of plant speciation). Consider the statement:

"Natural and artificial selection will preserve species biodiversity despite the effects of climate change."

Using the source material and your own knowledge, discuss your opinion in an essay of 2½–3 pages. You are expected to: read the sources carefully; take a definite stand; plan your essay before writing (the plan is marked); present a debated argument using relevant information from Sources A–H plus your own Life Sciences knowledge; arrange the information to develop your argument; write in a scientifically appropriate way; and discuss at least nine different facts from the sources.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marked with the IEB essay rubric (40): Planning (6); Use of knowledge from sources (8); Use of own knowledge (4); Content relevance (2); Quality of argument supporting the decision (8); Fairness — counter-opinions integrated (4); Presentation (4); Scientific merit (4).

Examples of usable facts —
WILL preserve biodiversity: overall extinction increase is still relatively low (<1,4%) (C); new species evolved after every past mass extinction, e.g. many reptiles after the Permian extinction (C, F); ~60% of amphibian species hit by chytridiomycosis show signs of evolving resistance, e.g. Xenopus laevis (D); Gulf killifish evolved genetic resistance to pollutants, and corals and tawny owls have adapted to rising temperatures (D); natural selection can act quickly — up to four times faster than previously thought (F); polyploidy raises variation (up to 80% of plants are polyploid) (D); humans facilitate allopatric speciation by introducing species and fragmenting habitat, e.g. the London Underground mosquito and the helicopter dragonfly (H); more new plant species have appeared in Britain than are known to have gone extinct in all of Europe (H); artificial selection has produced coral varieties that withstand hotter, more acidic water (G).
WILL NOT preserve biodiversity: climate-change effects — forest fires, storms, droughts, rising seas — cause habitat loss and mass deaths, and modern climate change is extreme and rapid (A); the IPCC warns up to one-sixth of species could go extinct and we may be entering a 6th mass extinction (A); the Bramble Cay melomys was the first mammal made extinct by climate change (C); green sea turtle populations are skewed by too few males being born (C); current extinction rates are far above the background rate and rising sharply over the last 100–150 years (C); past mass extinctions and recoveries took very long periods (C); there are too many species to save them all (B); loss of keystone species triggers many further extinctions (E); ~40% of amphibians are still not resistant to chytridiomycosis and 18% have gone extinct (D); evolution is usually slow, especially for long-generation species (D); few animals are polyploid (D); artificial selection is expensive and works on only one species at a time (G).
